newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Beleaguered Serbian president offers reforms.
newsitem.headline: Beleaguered Serbian president offers reforms.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, under mounting pressure at home and abroad, has called for economic reforms, a cabinet reshuffle and settling of political disputes in a democratic manner.
But opposition leaders flew off to Italy for talks on Friday, a day after European institutions stepped up pressure on Milosevic to concede November municipal elections.
Zajedno (Together) leaders Vuk Draskovic, Zoran Djindjic and Vesna Pesic left on a plane provided by Italy to confer with Prime Minister Romano Prodi and Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini.
As the Zajedno leaders left, Milosevic said in a statement to the state-run Tanjug news agency that a cabinet reshuffle was in the works.
But he maintained his silence on the election controversy that has posed the biggest challenge to his 10-year autocratic rule.

"The success of overall economic policy depends largely on personnel who will implement it in state bodies as well as in economy and finances," Tanjug quoted Milosevic as saying after meeting Serbian Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic.
"This implies an appropriate government reshuffle," he said, without indicating when the changes would occur.
"Political and inter-party disputes ought to be settled in a constructive and democratic manner," he added.

Milosevic's statement came after the West tightened the screws on him and his ruling Socialist Party (SPS) to reinstate victories by the Zajedno candidates in 14 of Serbia's 18 biggest cities, including the capital Belgrade and the second biggest city, Nis.

The 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said in Vienna that Milosevic should stop making piecemeal concessions to the opposition and should respect their electoral victories in the November 17 elections.

"Instead of seemingly giving concessions as the government is doing, the situation is much more simple -- they need to abide by the results of the elections...and give seats to the people who won the elections," the OSCE chairman, Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen, told a news conference.
Electoral commissions in Belgrade and Nis have ordered the opposition victories restored, but Socialist hardliners say they will challenge this.
The European Parliament in Strasbourg passed a resolution saying the European Union and its individual member countries should freeze relations with Serbia until democracy has been established there.
The Zajedno leaders have said little about the purpose of their visit to Italy and one senior Western diplomat expressed scepticism that any breakthrough would come of it.
"I don't think anything is likely to come from it because the ball is in the Serbian government's court and not in Zajedno's," the diplomat said. "I don't expect any major events or statements."
The diplomat added that Milosevic's talk of a cabinet reshuffle seemed ill-timed.
"I would have thought they would wait until this issue was resolved and then reorganise the government," the diplomat said. "But they are always full of their own surprises."
The Zajedno leaders left for Italy after speaking to a relatively modest crowd of 10,000 to 15,000 people who demonstrated in Belgrade on the 60th day of protests across Serbia.
The protests have drawn crowds of up to half a million people.
